generatedClaims: A distributor is considered the provider of a high-risk AI system when it puts its name or trademark on a high-risk AI system already placed on the market or put into service, unless contractual arrangements allocate the obligations otherwise.

The instructions for use must state the high-risk AI system’s level of accuracy, including the accuracy metrics it was tested and validated against, and any known or foreseeable circumstances that could affect that expected level of accuracy; they must also include the system’s level of robustness and cybersecurity, with the same “known or foreseeable circumstances” caveat.
The accompanying instructions for use must declare the levels of accuracy and the relevant accuracy metrics for high-risk AI systems.

Baseline rule: the obligation applies at first use of the high-risk AI system. If, during use, any element listed in paragraph 1 has changed or is no longer up to date, the deployer must take the necessary steps to update the information.

A market surveillance authority may request access to the source code of a high-risk AI system only on a reasoned request, and only if both conditions are met: access is necessary to assess conformity with Chapter III, Section 2 requirements, and testing, auditing, or verification based on the provider’s data and documentation have been exhausted or proved insufficient.
Any natural or legal person with grounds to consider that there has been an infringement of the Regulation may submit a complaint to the relevant market surveillance authority.
No. Filing a complaint with the relevant market surveillance authority is separate from seeking compensation; the provision preserves other administrative or judicial remedies.
Providers of general-purpose AI models placed on the market before 2 August 2025 must comply with the Regulation by 2 August 2027.
